કથા. Stories of this coast

Kathas of a word kept

Kathiawar has always kept its accounts as stories. A man gives his word, the word is tested, and what he does then is remembered longer than his name. Jhaverchand Meghani walked this country writing such stories down. These are ours.

NKovaya

A katha is a story told aloud. The old ones of this country are about tek, the vow a person will not break, and vachan, the word once given. They open with a duha, two lines that carry the whole matter before the telling begins.

We have told eight things from our own record in that manner. The couplets are ours. The facts are from the record, and every katha ends by stating them plainly, so that you can see where the telling stops and the record begins.

  1. One excavator2015. Six people, one machine, and a promise with three parts.
  2. The midnight call2017. The phone rang at twelve. Ninety minutes later the plant was running.
  3. The word, written down2019. The year the promise was written down as a method.
  4. Eight hundred tonnesSteel, two piling rigs and 150 workers, without one phone call to the client.
  5. Two plants at once2022. Two cement plants cold at the same time, served from one yard.
  6. Twenty-five minutesKiln down. One crew was five hours away. The other was at the gate.
  7. Sixty thousand cubic metresSixty thousand cubic metres of concrete on a coast that eats concrete.
  8. ZeroTwenty-five lakh hours of work, and every worker went home.

The man who walked Kathiawar

Jhaverchand Meghani

Gujarati folk literature, 1896 to 1947

He walked Kathiawar from village to village with a notebook and wrote down what the bards and the grandmothers remembered, before it could be lost. The result was the five volumes of Saurashtra ni Rasdhar. Gandhi called him the national poet. Most of his heroes were not kings. They were ordinary people who had given their word and would not take it back.

What we tookA firm is the promises it kept on the days when keeping them was expensive. We write ours down with their dates, and we call them kathas.

2015. Kovaya

One excavator

Six people, one machine, and a promise with three parts.

2 min read

NKovaya
On this page
  1. What the record says
Kathas
  • Kathas overview

The kathas

  • One excavator
  • The midnight call
  • The word, written down
  • Eight hundred tonnes
  • Two plants at once
  • Twenty-five minutes
  • Sixty thousand cubic metres
  • Zero

Listen. This is not a story about a company. In 2015 there was no company. There was a village called Kovaya on a white shore, a cement works that never slept, and one excavator.

One excavator is not much. A plant of that size has more machines in its scrapyard. A bank would have looked at that machine and seen one asset, already depreciating. But the six who stood round it saw something a bank does not count. They were here. They lived where the work was. When the plant’s own night was at its worst, they were a walk away.

The man who had brought them together did not stand apart from them with a notebook. He sat in the cab. He dug with the crew, ate with the crew, and went home as dusty as the crew. On this coast a man is watched before he is trusted, and the plant watched him. It saw who was still there at the end of the shift.

Now hear the promise, for it had three parts, and nothing has been added to it since.

Never miss a deadline. If the trench is promised for the twentieth, it is ready on the twentieth. Not on the twenty-first, with reasons.

Never compromise on quality. What is built will be loaded, shaken and salted for thirty years by people who never met the builder. It is built for them.

Never burden the client with operational noise. The client has a plant to run. He is not to be telephoned about a puncture, a missing fitter or a quarrel between two drivers. Those are ours to carry.

In Kathiawar they call such a thing a tek. It is not a target. A target is something you hope to reach. A tek is something you would be ashamed to be seen without.

Six people cannot do very much in a day. But six people who keep their word are asked back the next day, and the day after that there is work for seven.

That is all that happened in 2015. One machine worked. A promise was made at a gate, by people the gatekeeper knew by name. Everything that came afterwards, the three hundred machines and the six hundred hands, came through that gate and by that promise.

2017

The midnight call

The phone rang at twelve. Ninety minutes later the plant was running.

2 min read

NCement works, Kovaya
On this page
  1. What the record says
Kathas
  • Kathas overview

The kathas

  • One excavator
  • The midnight call
  • The word, written down
  • Eight hundred tonnes
  • Two plants at once
  • Twenty-five minutes
  • Sixty thousand cubic metres
  • Zero

There is an hour on this coast when the road is empty and the sea can be heard from the village. The fishing boats are out or asleep. The lions are walking. The only things awake are the kilns and the men who mind them.

At that hour, in 2017, a telephone rang in Kovaya.

What had failed inside the plant does not matter now, and the plant’s name is not ours to tell. What matters is what a breakdown is. A cement plant is one long chain from the quarry to the ship. Stop one link and every link behind it backs up, and every link in front of it starves. The loss is not counted by the day. It is counted by the minute, and somebody is counting.

So a man in a control room looked at a list of names. Most of the names on such a list belong to firms in cities. They are good firms. They will send a crew. The crew will arrive tomorrow.

He rang the name that was next door.

By then the firm in Kovaya was no longer six people. Owners of machines had begun to stand with it, and men who had spent their lives moving heavy loads along this coast. It was the first shape of what would become the network. And on this night it meant that when the phone rang, the right people could be woken by walking to their doors.

They did not ask whether an order had been raised. They did not ask what the rate would be at that hour. They went.

Ninety minutes after the telephone rang, the repair was finished.

Understand what that sentence says. It does not say that they arrived in ninety minutes. It says that inside ninety minutes they had arrived, been admitted, understood the fault, done the work and stood back.

In the morning the day shift came in to a plant that was running, and some of them never knew it had stopped.

A plant remembers a night like that. Not in a certificate. In a habit. The next time something failed after dark, nobody looked at the list.

What the record says

Year
2017
The network
Machinery owners and logistics veterans had begun to join.
The call

The result
The firm’s first emergency repair, completed within ninety minutes of the call

2019

The word, written down

A promise kept by habit dies with the people who have the habit. In 2019 it was cut into a method.

2 min read

NKovaya
On this page
  1. What the record says
Kathas
  • Kathas overview

The kathas

  • One excavator
  • The midnight call
  • The word, written down
  • Eight hundred tonnes
  • Two plants at once
  • Twenty-five minutes
  • Sixty thousand cubic metres
  • Zero

A hundred and twenty kilometres from Kovaya, at the foot of Girnar, there is a boulder the size of a house. Twenty-two centuries ago a king had his word cut into it. He did not trust it to messengers, who forget, or to governors, who improve things. He put it in stone, in the speech of ordinary people, beside the road where they would pass.

The firm at Kovaya came to the same thought in 2019, for the same reason.

By then more than eighty tradesmen answered its call. Consulting engineers had joined, so that a drawing could be questioned before it was built. The work had grown past what one person could watch.

And that is the dangerous year in the life of any firm that has done well. The founder can no longer be on every site. The promise that was kept because he was standing there must now be kept where he is not. Most firms fail at exactly this place. The first ten jobs are done by the best people with the owner watching. The eleventh is done by whoever is free.

So they sat down and asked a hard question. What do we actually do, when it goes well?

Not what they believed. What they did. Who speaks to the client, and who does not. What is written down at the end of each shift. What happens before a machine is allowed through the gate. Who may say yes to a change, and who must say no.

They wrote the answers out in order, and they gave the result a plain name: the Zero-Interference Delivery Model.

The name says who it is for. It is not for the firm’s convenience. It is for the man who runs the plant, who has given the work to someone precisely so that he need not think about it again. One contract. One project manager with the authority to deploy. One daily report. And between those, silence.

A method is a humbler thing than a legend. Nobody sings about a checklist. But a legend cannot be handed to a new supervisor on his first morning, and a method can.

From that year, a job done by people the founder had never met was done the way he would have done it. That is the only kind of growth worth having.

A plant expansion

Eight hundred tonnes, and silence

Steel, two piling rigs and 150 workers went through a plant gate. The client’s telephone did not ring once.

2 min read

NCement works, Kovaya
On this page
  1. What the record says
Kathas
  • Kathas overview

The kathas

  • One excavator
  • The midnight call
  • The word, written down
  • Eight hundred tonnes
  • Two plants at once
  • Twenty-five minutes
  • Sixty thousand cubic metres
  • Zero

How do you measure a job?

By the tonnes, people say. By the cubic metres. By the days. Those are honest measures, and we keep them. But there is another, and it is the one the old contractors of this coast would have understood best. You measure a job by what the other man did not have to do.

Hear what was asked. A plant was to be made larger. Before anything could rise, the ground had to be made ready to carry it. That meant piles, and piles meant two piling rigs, which are not machines you bring down a village lane in the afternoon. It meant reinforcement: eight hundred tonnes of steel bar, which is a great many trailers, each to be received, checked, unloaded and stacked where the fixers could reach it. And it meant a hundred and fifty workers, each with a gate pass, a helmet, an induction, a place to eat and a way home.

Now think of the telephone calls that such a mobilisation makes, in the ordinary way.

The trailer is at the gate and security will not let it in. The rig has arrived but the crane to assemble it has not. Forty men are here and their passes are not. Where shall we stack the steel? The driver wants to know who will sign.

Every one of those calls lands on a plant engineer who has his own work. Twenty calls a day for a month. That is the hidden price of a contractor, and it is on no invoice.

It was all done. The steel came, and was stacked. The rigs came, and were raised. The hundred and fifty came, and were inducted, and went to work.

And the client was not telephoned. Not once.

There is no trick in it. There is only the knowledge of this particular ground: which gate, which hour, which form, which weighbridge, which officer signs. A firm from far away must ask. A firm that has lived beside the gate for years already knows.

The old word for it is maryada: knowing the limits of another man’s house, and keeping your noise inside your own.

2022

Two plants at once

A shutdown is a battle against a fixed sunset. In 2022 there were two of them at the same time.

2 min read

NCement works, Kovaya
On this page
  1. What the record says
Kathas
  • Kathas overview

The kathas

  • One excavator
  • The midnight call
  • The word, written down
  • Eight hundred tonnes
  • Two plants at once
  • Twenty-five minutes
  • Sixty thousand cubic metres
  • Zero

Once a year a cement plant lets its kiln go cold. It is not rest. It is the opposite of rest. For that fixed number of days everything that could not be touched while the fire burned must be opened, repaired and closed again. Brick is cut out and laid new. Steel is cut and welded. Men go into places that are closed to them for the rest of the year.

And the sun goes down on the last day whether you are finished or not. Every hour after that is an hour of cement not made.

Tolstoy tells of a peasant who was promised all the land he could walk round between sunrise and sunset. He walked too far. That is every shutdown that was ever planned badly.

In 2022 two plants on this coast went cold at the same time.

A firm that owns its machines cannot do it. Its cranes are at one plant or at the other. Its welders are in one kiln or the other. It must choose which client to disappoint.

But the firm at Kovaya had made a different choice years before, and had been called foolish for it. It did not own the fleet. It had bound to itself, one tested partner at a time, the owners of more than two hundred machines, each within reach, each proven on a live job. See Why we do not own three hundred machines.

So when two plants asked on the same days, the answer to both was yes.

Two project managers, each with the authority to deploy and each answering for one plant alone. Two streams of fitters, welders and riggers, shift after shift. Cranes for both. And behind both, the same yard, the same registers and the same people who are reachable at any hour.

Neither plant was told to wait for the other. That was the whole point.

By the end of that year something had changed that no order records. When a thing broke anywhere along this belt, in a cement plant or outside one, the first telephone call had a habit of coming to the same number.

Kiln down

Twenty-five minutes

One crew was five hours away. The other was already at the gate.

2 min read

NCement works, Kovaya
On this page
  1. What the record says
Kathas
  • Kathas overview

The kathas

  • One excavator
  • The midnight call
  • The word, written down
  • Eight hundred tonnes
  • Two plants at once
  • Twenty-five minutes
  • Sixty thousand cubic metres
  • Zero

A kiln is a river of fire in a steel pipe, turning slowly, day and night, for months. When it is running you do not notice it, as you do not notice your own heart.

Then one day it stops.

Now the men in the control room are doing sums. So many tonnes an hour, not made. So many hours to cool before anyone can go in. So many to repair. So many to heat again, slowly, because brick that is hurried will crack. They add it up and they give the manager a figure: this is when we shall be running again. That figure is called the projected recovery. Everyone hates it.

Two firms could be called.

One was a good firm in a city. It said, truthfully, that its crew would need at least five hours to reach the plant. Nobody could blame it. That is how far away the city is.

The other was at Kovaya.

Twenty-five minutes after the call, its people were on site.

Do not think of twenty-five minutes as a fast drive. Think of what must already be true for it to be possible. The supervisor must know the gate. The gate must know the supervisor. The fitters must hold passes that have not lapsed. The crane’s owner must answer his telephone. The helmets must be in the vehicle and the vehicle must have fuel. Twenty-five minutes is not speed. It is ten years of being ready, spent in one night.

And here is what the old storytellers would call the turn of the tale. The four hours and thirty-five minutes between the two firms did not stay four hours and thirty-five minutes. Work begun early finishes early, and what finishes early lets the next thing begin. The gain grew as it went.

The plant was running again eight hours before the figure everyone hated.

Eight hours of a kiln. Ask any plant manager what he would give for that.

The event

Our team on site
25 minutes after the call
The alternative

The result
The plant resumed production eight hours ahead of its projected recovery.

Concrete against the sea

Sixty thousand cubic metres

On this coast the wind brings salt to every structure, every day. Sixty thousand cubic metres of our concrete stand in it.

2 min read

NCement works, Kovaya
On this page
  1. What the record says
Kathas
  • Kathas overview

The kathas

  • One excavator
  • The midnight call
  • The word, written down
  • Eight hundred tonnes
  • Two plants at once
  • Twenty-five minutes
  • Sixty thousand cubic metres
  • Zero

There is an enemy on this coast that does not sleep, does not strike, and is never seen. It is carried in the air.

Stand at Jafrabad and watch the salt pans. The same sun and the same wind that turn sea water into white heaps are at work on everything else as well. Salt settles on steel and the steel reddens. It settles on concrete, and the concrete drinks it, a little deeper each monsoon, until it reaches the bars inside. Then the bars rust. Rust is larger than iron. It swells, and it bursts the concrete from within, and one morning a piece the size of a plate falls off a column that looked sound the day before.

Every building here is under that siege from the hour it is cast.

Now, concrete is a strange thing to be proud of. Nobody admires a foundation. It is poured, it is buried, and a crusher that shakes like an earthquake is bolted on top of it. If the builder did his work, the foundation is never thought of again. That is the only praise it gets.

So how do you build what must never be thought of again, in air that is trying to dissolve it?

You do it by refusing every easy thing. You do not use the sand that is nearest, because the nearest sand has the sea in it. You make the mix dense, and you blend the cement so that the concrete closes its pores. You add what resists corrosion. You put more cover over the steel than a builder inland would trouble with. You cast cubes from every pour and you send them to an accredited laboratory, and you wait for the result before you say the word finished.

And when the pour is a great one, more than a thousand cubic metres placed in one unbroken effort, you watch its temperature like a physician, because a mass that heats too fast cracks in its own heart.

None of this can be seen in the finished work. That is the test of it. Meghani’s heroes did their bravest things where no one was watching.

Since 2015, more than sixty thousand cubic metres. Under crushers, under mills, under silos and roads. Not one structural failure.

The sea is still asking.

kathas.zero:
1. Home
  2. Kathas
  3. Zero

Every worker goes home

Zero

Twenty-five lakh hours of work. Of all the numbers in our ledger, the smallest is the one we guard most closely.

3 min read

NKovaya
On this page
  1. What the record says
Kathas
  • Kathas overview

The kathas

  • One excavator
  • The midnight call
  • The word, written down
  • Eight hundred tonnes
  • Two plants at once
  • Twenty-five minutes
  • Sixty thousand cubic metres
  • Zero

Fifteen hundred years ago a young man in this country wrote a book of numbers. The arithmetic in it runs on an idea that India gave to the world: that nothing can be written down, and counted with. A circle for emptiness. Zero.

It is the hardest number to keep.

Any firm can make a large number. Hire more men and the hours go up. Buy more cement and the cubic metres go up. But there is one figure in our books that only goes one way, and it is not the way we want. An accident cannot be taken back. One lost-time injury and the zero is gone, and no amount of work afterwards restores it.

So think what it means to hold that number at zero through two and a half million hours.

Two and a half million hours of men on scaffolds forty metres up. Of men inside silos, in the dark, standing on cement that may shift. Of welding sparks, of loads hanging from hooks, of tippers reversing, of trenches in rock, of kilns that were alight a day ago. Of May afternoons at forty-one degrees and monsoon mornings when every surface is slick.

It is not luck. Luck does not last two and a half million hours.

It is small things, done every single day by people who are tired of doing them. The talk before the shift, ten minutes, standing: What are we doing today? What can hurt us? What have we done about it? Who is new? The permit that must be signed before a spark is struck. The harness that is inspected and not merely worn. The certificate that says a man is fit to work at height, because a faint at forty metres has no second chapter. The audit, every week, by someone who does not report to the job.

And one rule above them. Any worker may stop the job. The newest helper, on his first morning, may put up his hand and say I do not like the look of that, and the work stops while someone looks. He will not be mocked. He will be thanked.

No date is worth a life. The leadership will stand behind any supervisor who refuses an unsafe instruction.

When the old bards of Kathiawar praised a man, they did not praise him for what he had won. They praised him for who was still alive because of him.

Every evening, six hundred homes along this coast have someone to wait for. That is the number.

The first midnight call

In 2017 a plant on this coast rang us at midnight. Ninety minutes later the repair was complete. It was the first emergency we had answered, and it decided what kind of firm we would become.

2 min read

NCement works, Kovaya
On this page

What the record says

Case note

2017
What
The firm’s first emergency plant repair
When
2017. The call came at midnight.
Result
Repair completed within 90 minutes of the call
What followed
A reputation, in one sentence, passed from one control room to the next

What the record does not say

It does not name the plant. It does not say what had failed, or how many people went. We could fill those gaps with colour, and the story would read better for it. We would rather leave them empty than fill them with something we cannot stand behind.

What we can tell you

We can tell you what kind of firm answered that call.

It was two years old. It had one founder who still worked beside the crew. It had, that year, begun to form its first alliances with machine owners and transport people: a small circle, chosen with care, who owned their equipment, knew the plants and answered their phones.

There was no emergency response service to speak of, and no rate card for one. There was a telephone that was answered, people who lived close enough to come, and a habit of finishing what was started.

What it changed

Word travels in this corridor the way it has always travelled, from one control room to the next. After that night it travelled in a particular form.

A reputation of that kind cannot be bought and is very easily lost. Every emergency since has been answered in the knowledge that the sentence has to stay true.

By 2022 we had become the de facto emergency response partner for several industries in the belt.

What it became

The habit of that night is now a written protocol. The few people the firm could call on then are now a network of supervisors, owners and crews spread through the villages round every plant. The ninety minutes have become a standing promise: under thirty minutes to site, anywhere in the belt, at any hour.

The telephone is still answered.

A kiln at a major cement plant broke down. Our civil and mechanical teams were on site within 25 minutes of the call. The plant resumed production 8 hours ahead of its projected recovery.

Why 25 minutes is possible

Nothing heroic is needed to reach a plant in 25 minutes. Nobody has to drive fast. That is the point.

Our supervisors live near the plants. The machines are parked a few kilometres away, with owners who give our calls priority. The crews are at home in the villages round the works. They have been inside these plants before and they know the gates.

A response is fast when nothing has to travel far. See Proximity.

Why both teams came

Kiln breakdowns are seldom tidy. A mechanical failure brings down refractory. A structural problem turns out to have a foundation under it. If the civil crew and the mechanical crew belong to different contractors, the first hours go in deciding whose problem it is.

Ours arrived together, as one firm, with one purpose: to get the plant running.

What eight hours are worth

We do not know that plant’s figures and would not publish them if we did. The arithmetic is simple enough to do for your own.

Take what your kiln produces in an hour. Multiply by eight. That is the clinker which exists because the repair finished early, and which would otherwise never have been made. See The arithmetic of a cold kiln.

What the record does not say

It does not name the plant or the year, and it does not describe the failure. Those belong to the client. See Why no client is named.

This is not an anecdote. It is the predictable outcome of strategic localisation.

Case note

2022
When

What
Shutdowns at two major cement plants, managed simultaneously
The network that year
More than 200 machines on call
What it showed
That the network had reached critical mass

Why it is the hardest thing we have done

One shutdown stretches a contractor. It needs hundreds of people in three shifts, cranes that are wanted in three places at once, and supervisors who can hold a schedule together when found work tears at it.

Two at once should be impossible for a firm of our size, by the usual arithmetic. A contractor with a fixed workforce and its own fleet would have had to split both down the middle and run each plant on half of what it needed.

Why it is possible

It is possible because of the way the firm is built.

A register, not a payroll
A second shutdown does not have to be staffed by thinning the first. People come from the register: tradesmen whose skill we have tested, called up for the window and stood down after it.
A network, not a fleet
Cranes and machines for a second plant come from owners who are not committed to the first.
Supervisors who know each plant
Each site is given its own core of people who have worked inside that plant before.
One standard
Every site runs under the same rules, the same permit discipline and the same daily report.

This is what the phrase “scale on demand” means when it is put to the test. See A network, by design.

What the record does not say

It does not name the plants, or the number of people at each, or the dates. It does not say that nothing went wrong, and we will not say so either. Shutdowns always meet surprises. What the record says is that both were managed, in the same weeks, by the same firm.

What it takes

Running two shutdowns at once follows three rules, and they are part of the shutdown playbook.

  • Preparation cannot be shared between two sites. Each needs its own scope walk, its own schedule and its own project manager.
  • The reserve for found work is held separately for each site, or the first surprise at one starves the other.
  • The leadership is reachable by both project managers at any hour.

Three flows, one plan

800 tonnes of steel
Thirty or so trailer loads. Each has to be ordered from the mill or the stockist, loaded, carried, weighed in, unloaded and stacked by size, in the order the bar benders need it. Steel that arrives too early rusts in the salt air. Steel that arrives too late stops the job.
Two piling rigs
Each travels on a low-loader, needs a prepared working platform, and has to find its first pile position marked and ready when it arrives.
150 workers
Each needs a medical, a gate pass, an induction, a place to sleep or a seat on a bus, and a supervisor who knows what they will be doing on the first morning.

Any one of these, run by a separate vendor, generates a dozen telephone calls to the client’s engineer. Where is the trailer? Who will unload it? The rig is at the gate and security will not admit it. Fifty of the workers have no passes.

Why the telephone does not ring

On a job run our way, all three flows are lines in one schedule, owned by one project manager, who has the authority to settle every one of those questions without asking anybody.

Steel is called forward when the cages are ready to be fixed. Rigs arrive when the platform is ready for them. Workers come when there is work for them to do. When one moves, the others move with it.

That is the whole of the Zero-Interference Doctrine in a single job.

Reading the record

The reasons

  1. What happens in a plant belongs to the plant

    A breakdown, a shutdown overrun, a cracked foundation: these are a client’s private business. A contractor who advertises having fixed them is advertising the client’s troubles.

  2. Our clients have not asked to be advertised

    Large companies control how their names and marks are used, and rightly. We do not use either without written permission.

  3. Discretion is part of the service

    The third promise is that we will not burden the client with operational noise. Talking about a client’s plant in public is noise of the loudest kind.

  4. The work should speak, and it can do so privately

    A reference given in person, by an engineer who has watched us work, is worth more than a logo.

What we do instead

On this site
We describe what we did, with the facts our record supports, and leave out who it was for. See Work on record.
In pre-qualification
We open the records behind our figures to your team.
On request
We arrange for you to speak to people who have worked with us, with their agreement.
On the ground
We take you to a site where we are working, with the permission of whoever owns it.

The neighbours we do name

This site names several companies on this coast: the cement works, the port, the shipyard, the terminals and the mill. They are named because they are the landscape. A portrait of Kovaya that left out the kilns would be dishonest.

Naming them says nothing about whether they are our clients, and no affiliation or endorsement is implied. Figures about them come from their own publications and from public records.

What we ask of you

The same discretion, in return. Our rates, our methods and the composition of our network are shared with clients in confidence. Our capability statement is marked confidential for that reason.

Photographs

We do not publish photographs taken inside a client’s plant. The pictures on this site are drawings, made for it. None of them shows a real plant.
